label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article II, Section 2, Clause 2. The President has power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, if two thirds of the senators present agree; he nominates and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoints ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, Supreme Court judges and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for; Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers in the President alone, in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments.
This story is about who picks the president's top aide.

On June 1, 1787 Wilson told the Convention that "The only powers he conceived strictly Executive were those of executing the laws, and appointing officers, not appertaining to and appointed by the Legislature."
In Federalist 77 (April 1788) Hamilton wrote, of the Senate's part in appointments, that "The consent of that body would be necessary to displace as well as to appoint."
From The Federalist No. 76 (Hamilton): “every advantage to be expected from such an arrangement would, in substance, be derived from the power of nomination.”
Miller takes the post from Susie Wiles.
Miller becomes the president's top aide.
The strongest argument against this is that a chief of staff may be an officer under this clause, so the Senate must share the choice.
We read this clause to mean the President can choose a functionary as top aide when Senate consent is not required.
Naming who helps execute the office stays with the appointing power this clause sets out.
